title: Sum of Array
description: Given an array of numbers, return the sum of all elements. The sum of an empty array is 0.
constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 1000. Each number is between -10^6 and 10^6.
hints: Keep a running total that starts at 0.
Loop over every element and add it to the total.

title: Clamp Value
description: Return n limited to the range from lo to hi (inclusive). If n is below lo return lo, if n is above hi return hi, otherwise return n.

examples.explanation: 15 is above the maximum, so the result is 10.

constraints: -10^9 <= n, lo, hi <= 10^9 and lo <= hi.
hints: Compare n with lo first.
Then compare n with hi. If neither limit applies, return n unchanged.

title: Leap Year Check
description: Return true if the given year is a leap year in the Gregorian calendar. A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except years divisible by 100, unless the year is also divisible by 400.

examples.explanation: 1900 is divisible by 100 but not by 400.
2000 is divisible by 400.

hints: Start with the divisible-by-4 rule.
Handle the century exceptions: divisible by 100 is not a leap year unless divisible by 400.

title: Digital Root
description: Repeatedly replace n with the sum of its digits until it has only one digit, then return that digit.
hints: Extract digits with n % 10 and Math.floor(n / 10).
Repeat the digit sum while the number still has two or more digits.

title: Greatest Common Divisor
description: Return the greatest common divisor of two non-negative integers a and b. gcd(a, 0) is a.

examples.explanation: 6 is the largest number dividing both 12 and 18.

constraints: 0 <= a, b <= 10^9 and a, b are not both 0.
hints: Euclid's idea: gcd(a, b) equals gcd(b, a % b).
Stop when the second number becomes 0.

title: Ordinal Suffix
description: Return the number followed by its English ordinal suffix, for example 1 becomes "1st", 2 becomes "2nd", 3 becomes "3rd" and 4 becomes "4th". Numbers ending in 11, 12 or 13 always use "th".

examples.explanation: 11 is a special case and uses th.
Ends in 2 and is not 12.

hints: Look at n % 100 first to catch 11, 12 and 13.
Otherwise use n % 10: 1 is st, 2 is nd, 3 is rd, everything else is th.

title: Base Converter
description: Convert a non-negative integer n to its representation in the given base (2 to 16). Use uppercase letters A-F for digits above 9. Do not add prefixes or leading zeros; 0 is "0".
hints: Repeatedly take n % base to get the lowest digit.
Build the string from the right, dividing n by the base each time, and special-case 0.

title: Trailing Zeros in Factorial
description: Return the number of trailing zeros in n! (n factorial). n can be large, so do not compute the factorial.

examples.explanation: 25! has 6 factors of 5 (5, 10, 15, 20 and 25 counts twice), giving 6 trailing zeros.

hints: A trailing zero comes from a factor of 10 = 2 * 5, and factors of 2 are plentiful.
Count factors of 5: add n/5, n/25, n/125, ... (integer division).

title: Title Case Words
description: Return the string with the first letter of every word uppercased and the remaining letters lowercased. Words are separated by single spaces; keep all spaces exactly as they appear in the input.

examples.explanation: Each word starts with a capital and the rest is lowercase.

constraints: 0 <= s.length <= 1000. s contains letters and spaces only.
hints: Split on " " so that extra spaces produce empty pieces you can keep.
For each non-empty word combine word[0].toUpperCase() with word.slice(1).toLowerCase(), then join with " ".

title: Camel to Snake Case
description: Convert a camelCase identifier to snake_case: before every uppercase letter that is not the first character insert an underscore, then lowercase every letter.

examples.explanation: Underscores go before V and N.

constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 100. s contains letters only.
hints: Walk through the characters one at a time.
An uppercase letter at index 0 gets no underscore; later ones get "_" plus the lowercase letter.

title: Caesar Cipher
description: Shift every letter of s forward in the alphabet by shift positions, wrapping around from z to a. shift may be negative (shift backward). Keep the case of each letter and leave non-letters unchanged.

examples.explanation: H becomes K, e becomes h, and so on; punctuation is unchanged.

hints: Use charCodeAt and String.fromCharCode, working relative to "a" or "A".
JavaScript's % can be negative, so normalise with ((x % 26) + 26) % 26.

title: Isogram Check
description: Return true if no letter appears more than once in s. Ignore case (A and a are the same letter) and ignore every character that is not a letter. The empty string is an isogram.

examples.explanation: Every letter is different.
The letter s appears twice.

hints: A Set remembers which letters you have already seen.
Lowercase the string and skip characters outside a-z.

title: Version Number Compare
description: Compare two version strings made of dot-separated non-negative integers. Return -1 if v1 is older than v2, 1 if v1 is newer, and 0 if they are equal. Compare segment by segment as numbers (so "1.10" is newer than "1.2"), and treat missing segments as 0.

examples.explanation: 2 < 10 in the second segment.
The missing segment counts as 0.

constraints: Each version has 1 to 10 segments; each segment is an integer between 0 and 10^6 and may have leading zeros.
hints: Split both strings on "." and convert the pieces to numbers.
Loop to the longer length, using 0 when a version has run out of segments.

title: Decode Bracketed Repeats
description: An encoded string uses the rule k[text], meaning text repeated k times. Rules can be nested. Return the decoded string. k is a positive integer and the input is always valid.

examples.explanation: 2[c] is cc, so a2[c] is acc, repeated 3 times.

constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 100. s has lowercase letters, digits and brackets. The decoded length is at most 1000.
hints: Use two stacks: one for repeat counts and one for the strings built so far.
On "[" push the current count and string and start fresh; on "]" pop and append the current string repeated count times.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
description: Return the longest substring of s that reads the same forwards and backwards. If several have the same length, return the one that starts earliest.

examples.explanation: "bab" and "aba" both work; "bab" starts first.

constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 1000. s contains lowercase letters.
hints: Every palindrome grows outward from a center: a character or the gap between two characters.
Try each center, expand while both ends match, and keep the result only when it is strictly longer.

title: Text Justification
description: Format an array of words into lines of exactly maxWidth characters, fully justified. Pack as many words as fit on each line (one space minimum between words). Distribute extra spaces between words as evenly as possible, giving the leftmost gaps the extra ones. The last line, and any line with a single word, is left-justified and padded with spaces on the right. Return the array of lines.

examples.explanation: The first line has 3 gaps sharing 8 extra spaces evenly.

constraints: 1 <= words.length <= 300, 1 <= words[i].length <= maxWidth <= 100. Words contain no spaces.
hints: Greedily pick the words for a line while total length plus minimum single spaces stays within maxWidth.
For a full line compute spaces = maxWidth - letters, base = floor(spaces / gaps), and the first (spaces % gaps) gaps get one more.

title: Shortest Palindrome by Prepending
description: You may add characters only in front of string s. Return the shortest palindrome you can obtain this way.

examples.explanation: Adding "dcb" in front gives a palindrome, and nothing shorter works.

constraints: 0 <= s.length <= 5000. s contains lowercase letters.
hints: The answer is reverse(part that is not covered) + s, so find the longest palindromic prefix of s.
Build s + "#" + reverse(s) and use a prefix-function (KMP failure table) to find the longest prefix matching a suffix.

title: Count Positive Numbers
description: Given an array of integers, return the number of positive integers in the array.

examples.explanation: There are three positive numbers.

constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 1000
hints: Zero is not positive, so use a strict comparison.
Keep a counter and increase it for every element greater than 0.

title: Alternating Sign Sum
description: Return nums[0] - nums[1] + nums[2] - nums[3] + ... , alternating the sign starting with plus. The result for an empty array is 0.
constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 1000. Each number is between -10^6 and 10^6.
hints: The sign depends on whether the index is even or odd.
Add nums[i] at even indices and subtract it at odd indices.

title: Peak Elements
description: Return, in increasing order, the indices of all peaks in nums. An element is a peak if it is strictly greater than both its left and right neighbours. The first and last elements are never peaks.
constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 1000. Each number is between -10^6 and 10^6.
hints: Only indices 1 to n-2 can be peaks.
Compare nums[i] with nums[i-1] and nums[i+1] using strict greater-than.

title: Invert Object Keys and Values
description: Given an object whose values are all unique strings, return a new object in which every original value becomes a key and every original key becomes its value.

examples.explanation: Each key/value pair is swapped.

constraints: 0 <= number of keys <= 100. All values are unique strings.
hints: Object.entries(obj) gives you [key, value] pairs.
Build a new object and set result[value] = key for each pair.

title: Pick and Omit Keys
description: Given an object, a list of key names and a mode, return a new object. If mode is "pick", keep only the listed keys that exist in the object. If mode is "omit", keep every key except the listed ones. Names in the list that are not in the object are ignored.

examples.explanation: Only a and c are kept.

constraints: 0 <= number of keys in obj <= 100. keys has at most 100 strings and may include names missing from obj. mode is either "pick" or "omit".
hints: Put the listed keys in a Set for fast lookup.
Loop over Object.entries(obj) and keep an entry when (in the set) matches (mode is pick).

title: Symmetric Difference of Arrays
description: Given two arrays of integers, return a sorted (ascending) array of the distinct values that appear in exactly one of the two arrays.

examples.explanation: 2 and 3 appear in both arrays, so only 1 and 4 remain.

constraints: 0 <= a.length, b.length <= 1000. Each element is an integer between -10^6 and 10^6.
hints: Turn each array into a Set to drop duplicates.
Collect values missing from the other set, then sort numerically with (p, q) => p - q.

title: Pairs to Object with Duplicate Keys
description: Given an array of [key, value] pairs where keys may repeat, return an object that maps each key to an array of all its values, in the order the pairs appear.

examples.explanation: The key a appears twice, so its values are collected into one array.

constraints: 0 <= pairs.length <= 1000. Keys are non-empty strings. Values are integers.
hints: Destructure each pair with for (const [key, value] of pairs).
Create the array the first time you see a key, then push the value.

title: Highest Scoring Student
description: Given an array of student records, each with a name and a score, return the name of the student with the highest score. If several students share the highest score, return the one who appears first. If the array is empty, return an empty string.

examples.explanation: Ben and Cy tie at 92, and Ben appears first.

constraints: 0 <= records.length <= 1000. Each name is a non-empty string. Each score is an integer between -1000 and 1000.
hints: Track the best record seen so far while looping.
Replace it only when a score is strictly greater, so ties keep the earlier student.

title: Merge Objects Summing Numbers
description: Given two objects whose values are all integers, return a new object containing every key that appears in either object. If a key appears in both, its value in the result is the sum of the two values.

examples.explanation: Only b appears in both objects, so its values 2 and 3 are added.

constraints: 0 <= number of keys in each object <= 100. Keys are non-empty strings. Values are integers between -10^6 and 10^6.
hints: Start from a copy of the first object, for example with the spread syntax {...a}.
For each entry of the second object, add its value to the existing value, or to 0 when the key is new.

title: Sum Sales by Category
description: Given an array of sale records, each with a category and an amount, return an object that maps every category to the total of its amounts.

examples.explanation: The two toys sales add up to 17.

constraints: 0 <= sales.length <= 1000. Each category is a non-empty string. Each amount is an integer between -10^6 and 10^6.
hints: Destructure each record with for (const { category, amount } of sales).
Add the amount to the running total for that category, starting from 0 the first time you see it.

title: Unique Tags Across Records
description: Given an array of records, each with an id and an array of tag strings, return a sorted array of the distinct tags that appear in any record. Sort in the default string order (plain alphabetical for lowercase words).

examples.explanation: web appears twice but is listed once, and the result is sorted.

constraints: 0 <= records.length <= 1000. Each record has 0 to 20 tags. Tags are non-empty lowercase strings.
hints: Add every tag to a Set so duplicates disappear.
Spread the Set into an array with [...set] and call .sort() on it.

title: Deep Merge Objects
description: Given two JSON objects a and b, return a new object that merges them deeply. If a key exists in both and both values are plain objects (not arrays, not null), merge those two values recursively. In every other case where a key exists in both, the value from b wins. Arrays are replaced, never concatenated. Keys that exist in only one object are kept as they are.

examples.explanation: Key b is an object in both, so it is merged: y is taken from b and z is added. Keys a and c appear only once.

constraints: Nesting depth is at most 10. Each object has at most 50 keys per level. Values are numbers, strings, booleans, null, arrays or objects.
hints: Write a small helper that tells whether a value is a plain object: not null, typeof 'object', and not an array.
Copy every key of a, then for each key of b either recurse (both plain objects) or overwrite.

title: Flatten Nested Object Keys
description: Given a nested JSON object, return a flat object whose keys are the dotted paths to each leaf value. A leaf is any value that is not a plain object; arrays and null count as leaves and are kept unchanged. Nested objects are never empty, and no key contains a dot.

examples.explanation: The path to the value 3 goes through b, then d, then e.

constraints: Nesting depth is at most 10. The object has at most 200 leaves in total. Keys are non-empty strings without dots.
hints: Write a recursive helper that carries the path built so far.
When a value is a plain object, recurse with path + '.' + key. Otherwise store it under the full path.

title: Unflatten Dotted Keys
description: Given a flat object whose keys are dotted paths, return the nested object those paths describe. A key without a dot stays at the top level. Values are never plain objects (they may be numbers, strings, booleans, null or arrays), and no key is a prefix path of another key.

examples.explanation: The path b.d.e creates b, then d inside it, then stores 3 under e.

constraints: 0 <= number of keys <= 200. Every path has at most 10 parts. Path parts are non-empty strings without dots.
hints: Split each key on '.' to get its parts.
Walk down from the result object, creating an empty object for each missing part except the last, then store the value under the last part.

title: Group Anagrams
description: Given an array of lowercase words, group together the words that are anagrams of each other. Return an array of groups. Inside each group, sort the words in default string order and keep every copy of a repeated word. Sort the groups themselves by their first word in default string order.

examples.explanation: eat, tea and ate share the same letters, as do tan and nat. Groups are ordered by first word: ate, bat, nat.

constraints: 0 <= words.length <= 1000. Each word has 1 to 20 lowercase letters. Words may repeat.
hints: Two words are anagrams when their sorted letters are equal, so use the sorted letters as a Map key.
After grouping, sort each group, then sort the list of groups by group[0].

title: Inner Join Records on Key
description: Given two arrays of record objects, left and right, and the name of a key present in every record, return the inner join. For every left record, in order, and for every right record with the same key value, in order, output one merged object made from all fields of the left record and all fields of the right record. If both records have the same field other than the key, the right record's value wins. Left records with no match produce nothing.

examples.explanation: Results follow the order of the left array.

constraints: 0 <= left.length, right.length <= 500. Every record contains the key, and its value is a string or an integer. Several records on either side may share a key value.
hints: Index the right records in a Map from key value to an array of records.
For each left record, look up its matches and push {...left, ...right} for each one.

title: Nested Path Lookup with Default
description: Given a JSON value obj, an array path of steps and a defaultValue, follow the path through obj and return the value found at the end. Use a string step to enter an object and an integer step to enter an array. If a step is missing, is out of range, is the wrong kind for the current value, or the current value is not an object or array, return defaultValue. A value of null found at the end of the path is a real value and is returned as is. An empty path returns obj itself.

examples.explanation: user is an object key, tags is an object key, and 1 is an index into the array.

constraints: path has at most 20 steps. Each step is a non-empty string or a non-negative integer. obj has nesting depth at most 20.
hints: Keep a current pointer and move it one step at a time, returning defaultValue as soon as a step fails.
Check that the current value is a non-null object, that arrays get numeric steps and objects get string steps, and use hasOwnProperty so that a step like "length" on an array counts as missing.

title: Deep Equality of JSON Values
description: Given two JSON values a and b, return true if they are deeply equal and false otherwise. Objects are equal when they have exactly the same keys with deeply equal values, regardless of key order. Arrays are equal when they have the same length and deeply equal items in the same order. An array is never equal to an object, and a missing key is never equal to a key whose value is null.

examples.explanation: Both objects have the same keys and values, only the key order differs.

constraints: Nesting depth is at most 20. Each value has at most 1000 items in total. Values are numbers, strings, booleans, null, arrays or objects.
hints: Handle primitives and null first, then arrays, then objects.
For objects, compare the number of keys, then check that every key of a exists in b with a deeply equal value.

title: LRU Cache Simulation
description: Simulate a least-recently-used (LRU) cache with a fixed capacity. Each operation is either ["put", key, value] or ["get", key]. A put stores the value (replacing the old value if the key already exists) and marks the key as the most recently used. A get returns the stored value, or -1 if the key is absent, and marks a found key as the most recently used. When a put makes the cache hold more than capacity keys, remove the least recently used key. Return the results of the get operations, in order.

examples.explanation: Getting key 1 makes it recent, so adding key 3 evicts key 2, and the later get of key 2 returns -1.

constraints: 1 <= capacity <= 100. 0 <= operations.length <= 1000. Keys and values are integers between 0 and 10^6.
hints: A JavaScript Map remembers insertion order, so its first key is always the oldest one.
To mark a key as recent, delete it and set it again. To evict, delete map.keys().next().value.

title: Inverted Word Index
description: Given an array of documents (strings made of letters and spaces), build an inverted index: an object that maps every word, converted to lowercase, to the sorted array of the distinct 0-based indices of the documents that contain it. Words are separated by one or more spaces, and a document may be empty.

examples.explanation: Words are lowercased, so The and the are the same word. Each index is listed once per word.

constraints: 0 <= docs.length <= 200. Each document has at most 200 characters, made of letters and spaces only.
hints: Lowercase each document, split it on ' ' and skip the empty pieces.
Because documents are processed in order, add an index only if it is not already the last index stored for that word.

title: Deep Diff of Two JSON Objects
description: Compare two JSON objects a and b and return the list of differences. A path is the dotted list of keys from the top object down to a value. For every key: if it exists only in a, output {"path": p, "type": "removed", "from": value}. If it exists only in b, output {"path": p, "type": "added", "to": value}. If it exists in both and both values are plain objects (not arrays, not null), compare them recursively. Otherwise, if the two values are not deeply equal, output {"path": p, "type": "changed", "from": oldValue, "to": newValue}. Arrays are compared as whole values with deep equality and are never entered. An added or removed subtree is reported once, at its root. Return the records sorted by path in default string order.

examples.explanation: zip disappeared from address, age changed, and email is new. The records are sorted by path.

constraints: Nesting depth is at most 10. Each object has at most 50 keys per level. Keys are non-empty strings without dots. Values are numbers, strings, booleans, null, arrays or objects.
hints: Walk both objects together over the union of their keys, carrying the dotted path built so far.
Recurse only when both values are plain objects. Otherwise compare them with a deep-equality helper, then sort the finished list by path.

title: Resolve Config References with Cycle Detection
description: Given a config object whose values are strings, replace every reference written as ${name} with the fully resolved value of the config key name. A reference is a dollar sign, an opening brace, any characters other than a closing brace, and a closing brace. References can chain through other keys. Return an object with the same keys and the resolved strings. If a key cannot be resolved, because its text refers to an unknown name or its resolution reaches a reference cycle (including a key that refers to itself), its value in the result is null. Text that is not a complete reference is left unchanged.

examples.explanation: Both references in url are replaced by the values of host and port.

constraints: 0 <= number of keys <= 100. Key names are non-empty strings. Each value is a string of at most 200 characters, and every fully resolved string is at most 1000 characters.
hints: Resolve keys with a depth-first search that marks each key as visiting or done, and remember finished results so each key is resolved only once.
Reaching a key that is still visiting means a cycle, so that key cannot be resolved, and neither can any key that needs it. Use String.replace with a regular expression and a replacer function.

title: LFU Cache Simulation
description: Simulate a least-frequently-used (LFU) cache with a fixed capacity. Each operation is either ["put", key, value] or ["get", key]. Every successful get and every put on an existing key counts as one use of that key, and a newly inserted key starts with one use. When a put of a new key finds the cache already holding capacity keys, first remove the key with the fewest uses. If several keys tie for the fewest uses, remove the least recently used among them, where a key's most recent use is its latest get or put. A put on an existing key replaces its value and never evicts. With capacity 0 nothing is ever stored. Return the results of the get operations, in order, using -1 for a missing key.

examples.explanation: Key 1 has two uses and key 2 has one, so adding key 3 evicts key 2. The get of key 2 returns -1 and the get of key 3 returns 3.

constraints: 0 <= capacity <= 100. 0 <= operations.length <= 1000. Keys and values are integers between 0 and 10^6.
hints: Store for each key its value, its use count and the time of its last use, using an operation counter as the clock.
When eviction is needed, scan all entries and pick the lowest count, breaking ties by the smallest last-use time. Handle capacity 0 first.

title: Counter with Closure Operations
description: A counter starts at 0. You are given an array of operations, each one of "inc" (add 1), "dec" (subtract 1), "reset" (set to 0) or "get" (read the current value). Process the operations in order and return an array with the value read by each "get", in order. The counter may go negative.

examples.explanation: The counter goes 1, 2 (read 2), 1 (read 1), then resets to 0 (read 0).

constraints: 0 <= operations.length <= 1000. Every operation is one of "inc", "dec", "reset" or "get".
hints: A closure lets a function keep a private variable between calls: write a makeCounter() that returns small functions sharing one count variable.
Call the matching function for each operation and collect the result only for "get".

title: Sort Strings by Length Then Alphabet
description: Given an array of strings, return a new array sorted by length from shortest to longest. Strings of equal length are ordered alphabetically using plain string comparison (code-unit order, so every uppercase letter comes before every lowercase letter). Keep repeated strings.

examples.explanation: fig has 3 letters, date, kiwi and pear have 4 (in alphabetical order), and apple has 5.

constraints: 0 <= words.length <= 1000. Each word has 1 to 30 letters.
hints: Array.prototype.sort accepts a comparator (a, b) => number. A negative result puts a first.
Compare lengths first, and only when they are equal compare the strings themselves with < and >.

title: Zip Arrays into Pairs
description: Given two arrays a and b, return an array of pairs where the i-th pair is [a[i], b[i]]. Stop at the length of the shorter array and ignore the extra items of the longer one.

examples.explanation: The shorter array has 2 items, so only 2 pairs are built.

constraints: 0 <= a.length, b.length <= 1000. Items are integers or strings.
hints: The number of pairs is Math.min(a.length, b.length).
Array.from({ length: k }, (_, i) => ...) builds an array of k items from the index.

title: Take While Prefix
description: Given an array of integers and the name of a rule, return the longest prefix of the array in which every item satisfies the rule. The rule is "positive" (item > 0), "even" (item is divisible by 2, and 0 counts as even) or "negative" (item < 0). Stop at the first item that fails the rule.

examples.explanation: 2 and 4 are even, and 5 stops the prefix, so 6 is not included even though it is even.

constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 1000. Each item is an integer between -10^6 and 10^6. rule is one of "positive", "even" or "negative".
hints: Store the three rules as small functions in an object and pick one by name.
Advance an index while the item passes, then return nums.slice(0, index).

title: Range with Step
description: Given integers start, end and step, return the array that begins at start and moves by step each time, stopping before it reaches or passes end (end itself is never included). The step may be negative to count down. If step is 0, or the step points away from end, return an empty array.

examples.explanation: The next value would be 12, which is past 10, so the range stops at 9.

constraints: -10^4 <= start, end <= 10^4. -10^4 <= step <= 10^4. The result has at most 1000 items.
hints: Handle step === 0 first, since it would loop forever.
Use one loop condition for positive steps (x < end) and another for negative steps (x > end).

title: Running Maximum
description: Given an array of integers, return an array of the same length where item i is the largest value among the first i + 1 items of the input.

examples.explanation: The maximum so far is 3, 3, 4, 4 and finally 5.

constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 1000. Each item is an integer between -10^6 and 10^6.
hints: Keep one variable holding the best value seen so far.
Start it at -Infinity so that any first item replaces it, and push it after every item.

title: Partition Array by Threshold
description: Given an array of integers and an integer threshold, return a two-item array [below, rest]. below holds the items smaller than the threshold and rest holds the items greater than or equal to it. Both keep the original relative order.

examples.explanation: 1 and 3 are below 5. The two 5s and the 8 are at least 5, in their original order.

constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 1000. Each item and the threshold are integers between -10^6 and 10^6.
hints: You can call filter twice, or loop once and push each item to one of two arrays.
Return the two arrays inside one outer array.

title: Memoization Call Counter
description: A recursive function fib(n) returns n when n < 2, and fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2) otherwise. It is wrapped in a memoizer that keeps one cache for the whole run: a call for an argument already in the cache returns the stored value without running the function body, and every recursive call also goes through the cache. You are given an array of arguments to call, in order. Return an object with two fields: results, the value returned for each call, and computations, the total number of times the function body actually ran across all calls.

examples.explanation: fib(5) runs the body for the arguments 0 to 5 (6 times). fib(3) is already cached. fib(7) adds only 6 and 7, so the total is 8.

constraints: 0 <= calls.length <= 100. Each argument is an integer between 0 and 40.
hints: Create a Map cache and a computations counter outside the recursive function so that they survive between calls.
Check the cache first. Only when it misses, increment the counter, compute the value with recursive calls to the same cached function, store it and return it.

title: Debounce Simulation
description: A debounced function runs only after events stop arriving for a while. You are given the times (in ms, in non-decreasing order) at which an event happens, and a wait time. Every event starts a timer that will fire at event time + wait, and it cancels the timer of the previous event if that timer has not fired yet. A timer fires unless another event arrives strictly before its fire time (an event arriving exactly at the fire time does not cancel it). Return the fire times, in order.

examples.explanation: The events at 0 and 100 are cancelled by the next event. The event at 150 fires at 350 because 400 is later than 350. The event at 400 fires at 600.

constraints: 0 <= events.length <= 1000. 0 <= events[i] <= 10^6 and the array is non-decreasing. 1 <= wait <= 10^6.
hints: An event's timer survives only if the next event is not strictly earlier than its fire time.
Compare each event with the next one, and treat the last event as always surviving.

title: Throttle Simulation
description: A throttled function runs at most once per wait period. You are given the times (in ms, in non-decreasing order) at which an event happens, and a wait time. The first event always runs. After that, an event runs only if at least wait ms have passed since the last event that ran (an event exactly wait ms later does run). Events that do not run are ignored and do not extend the period. Return the times of the events that ran, in order.

examples.explanation: 0 runs. 50 is too soon. 100 is exactly 100 ms after 0, so it runs. 120 is too soon after 100. 300 runs.

constraints: 0 <= events.length <= 1000. 0 <= events[i] <= 10^6 and the array is non-decreasing. 1 <= wait <= 10^6.
hints: Remember the time of the last event that actually ran, starting with nothing.
Run an event when nothing has run yet or when time - last >= wait, and update last only when you run it.

title: Event Emitter Simulation
description: Simulate an event emitter. Each operation is ["on", event, listenerId] to register a listener, ["off", event, listenerId] to remove it, or ["emit", event]. Listeners are called in the order they were registered. Registering a listener id that is already registered for the same event does nothing, and removing a listener that is not registered does nothing. For every "emit", record the array of listener ids that were called (an empty array if there are none). Return the recorded arrays in order.

examples.explanation: The first emit calls x and y. After x is removed, only y is called. Event b has no listeners.

constraints: 0 <= operations.length <= 1000. Event names and listener ids are non-empty strings.
hints: Keep a Map from event name to an array of listener ids.
Copy the array when you record an emit, so that later on/off operations do not change the recorded result.

title: Curried Function Evaluation
description: A curried sum function needs arity numbers in total, and it accepts them in several calls. Each call gives it a chunk of numbers. As soon as it has collected at least arity numbers, it returns the sum of the first arity numbers it received, and any extra numbers or later chunks are ignored. Until then it returns another function waiting for more. You are given arity and an array of chunks (each chunk is an array of numbers, possibly empty), to be passed in order as separate calls. Return the sum, or null if the chunks run out before arity numbers were collected.

examples.explanation: After the first chunk only one number is known. The second chunk completes the three numbers 1, 2 and 3.

constraints: 1 <= arity <= 20. 0 <= chunks.length <= 50. Each chunk has 0 to 20 integers between -1000 and 1000.
hints: Write curry(collected) that returns a function (...args) => ...; each call joins the new args to the collected ones.
If the joined list has at least arity numbers, return the sum of its first arity items. Otherwise return curry(joined) and pass the next chunk to that.

title: Sort Records by Multiple Keys
description: Given an array of record objects and a sort spec, return a new array with the records sorted. The spec is an array of [key, direction] pairs, where direction is "asc" or "desc". Records are compared by the first pair. If they tie, the next pair breaks the tie, and so on. Values under one key are all numbers or all strings; strings use plain code-unit order. Records that tie on every pair keep their original relative order, and an empty spec keeps the original order.

examples.explanation: a is sorted from high to low, so the two records with a = 2 come first, and they are ordered by n from low to high.

constraints: 0 <= records.length <= 1000. 0 <= spec.length <= 5. Every record has every key named in the spec.
hints: Write one comparator that loops over the spec and returns the first non-zero comparison.
For "desc" flip the sign of that comparison. Array.prototype.sort is stable, so returning 0 keeps the original order.

title: Reverse Vowels in String
description: Given a string, reverse the order of its vowels (a, e, i, o, u in lowercase or uppercase) and leave every other character exactly where it is. Each vowel keeps its own case when it moves.

examples.explanation: The vowels are e and o. Swapping their positions gives holle.

constraints: 0 <= s.length <= 1000. s contains only letters and spaces.
hints: Put one pointer at each end of the character array.
Move each pointer inward until it sits on a vowel, then swap the two vowels and move both pointers.

title: Squares of Sorted Array
description: Given an array of integers sorted in ascending order, return an array of the squares of each number, also sorted in ascending order. Aim for a solution that does not need a full sort.

examples.explanation: The squares are 16, 1, 0, 9, 100, and sorted they become 0, 1, 9, 16, 100.

constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 1000. Each item is an integer between -10^4 and 10^4, and the array is sorted in ascending order.
hints: The largest square is always at one of the two ends of the input.
Compare the absolute values at the two ends, and fill the result from the last position backwards.

title: Is Subsequence
description: Given two strings s and t, return true if s is a subsequence of t, meaning s can be obtained from t by deleting zero or more characters without changing the order of the rest. The empty string is a subsequence of every string.

examples.explanation: Deleting b and d from abcde leaves ace.

constraints: 0 <= s.length <= 100. 0 <= t.length <= 1000. Both strings contain lowercase letters only.
hints: Walk through t once, keeping a pointer into s.
Move the pointer in s forward only when the current character of t matches it, then check whether the pointer reached the end of s.

title: Max Sum of K Consecutive Elements
description: Given an array of integers and a window size k, return the largest sum of any k consecutive elements. If the array has fewer than k elements, return 0.

examples.explanation: The window sums are 8, 7, 9 and 6, and the largest is 9 (from 5, 1, 3).

constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 1000. 1 <= k <= 1000. Each item is an integer between -10^4 and 10^4.
hints: Compute the sum of the first k items once.
Slide the window by adding the item that enters and subtracting the item that leaves, and keep the best sum seen.

title: Maximum Consecutive Ones
description: Given an array containing only 0 and 1, return the length of the longest run of consecutive 1s. If there is no 1, return 0.

examples.explanation: The longest run of 1s is the last three items.

constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 1000. Each item is 0 or 1.
hints: Keep the length of the current run of 1s and the best run seen so far.
Add 1 to the current run on a 1, and reset it to 0 on a 0.

title: Equilibrium Index
description: Given an array of integers, return the leftmost index i such that the sum of the items to the left of i equals the sum of the items to the right of i. The item at i itself is not counted, and an empty side sums to 0. If no such index exists, return -1.

examples.explanation: Left of index 3 the sum is 1 + 7 + 3 = 11, and right of it the sum is 5 + 6 = 11.

constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 1000. Each item is an integer between -1000 and 1000.
hints: Compute the total sum first, then keep a running sum of the items to the left.
At index i the right sum is total - left - nums[i].

title: Minimum Start Value for Positive Prefix Sums
description: Given an array of integers, find the smallest positive integer startValue such that the running total startValue + nums[0] + ... + nums[i] is at least 1 for every i. If the array is empty, the answer is 1.

examples.explanation: The prefix sums are -3, -1, -4, 0, 2 and the lowest is -4, so we need a start value of at least 5 to stay at 1 or above.

constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 1000. Each item is an integer between -100 and 100.
hints: Only the lowest prefix sum matters, because the start value is added to every prefix sum.
If the lowest prefix sum is m, the answer is the larger of 1 and 1 - m.

title: Search Insert Position
description: Given a sorted array of distinct integers and a target, return the index of the target if it is in the array. If it is not, return the index where it would be inserted to keep the array sorted.

examples.explanation: 2 is not in the array, and inserting it at index 1 keeps the order 1, 2, 3, 5, 6.

constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 1000. The items are distinct integers sorted in ascending order, between -10^4 and 10^4. The target is an integer in the same range.
hints: Search for the first index whose value is greater than or equal to the target.
Keep lo and hi as a half-open range [lo, hi). If nums[mid] < target move lo to mid + 1, otherwise move hi to mid.

title: Integer Square Root
description: Given a non-negative integer n, return the largest integer r such that r * r <= n (the square root rounded down). Solve it with binary search, without using Math.sqrt or the ** operator.

examples.explanation: 2 * 2 = 4 is at most 8, but 3 * 3 = 9 is more than 8.

hints: The answer lies between 0 and n, and mid * mid grows as mid grows.
Use the upper middle, mid = floor((lo + hi + 1) / 2). If mid * mid <= n keep it as a candidate with lo = mid, otherwise hi = mid - 1.

title: Remove Adjacent Duplicates
description: Given a string, repeatedly remove a pair of two equal neighbouring characters until no such pair is left, and return the final string. The result does not depend on the order in which pairs are removed.

examples.explanation: Removing bb gives aaca, then removing aa gives ca, which has no equal neighbours.

constraints: 0 <= s.length <= 1000. s contains lowercase letters only.
hints: Use an array as a stack of the characters kept so far.
For each character, pop the stack if its top equals the character, otherwise push the character.

title: Backspace String Compare
description: Two strings are typed into empty text editors, where the character # means backspace. A backspace removes the character just before the cursor and does nothing when the text is empty. Return true if the two final texts are equal.

examples.explanation: Both strings end up as ac.

constraints: 0 <= s.length, t.length <= 200. Each string contains lowercase letters and the character #.
hints: Write a helper that builds the final text of one string with a stack.
Push every letter and pop on # (popping an empty stack changes nothing), then compare the two results.

title: Check If Array Is Rotated Sorted
description: Return true if the array is sorted in non-decreasing order, or could be made so by rotating it (moving some items from the front to the back without reordering them). Equal neighbours are allowed. An empty array counts as sorted.

examples.explanation: Rotating the array by 3 positions gives [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].

constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 1000. Each item is an integer between -10^4 and 10^4.
hints: Count the positions where an item is larger than the next one, treating the array as circular (the last item is followed by the first).
A sorted array that was rotated has at most one such drop.

title: Longest Ones After K Flips
description: Given an array of 0s and 1s and an integer k, you may flip at most k zeros into ones. Return the length of the longest run of consecutive 1s you can obtain.

examples.explanation: Flipping the zeros at indexes 5 and 10 makes indexes 5 to 10 all ones, which is six in a row.

constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 1000. Each item is 0 or 1. 0 <= k <= 1000.
hints: Look for the longest window that contains at most k zeros.
Grow the window on the right, and when the zero count goes above k, move the left edge forward until it is back to k.

title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
description: Given a positive integer target and an array of positive integers, return the smallest length of a contiguous subarray whose sum is at least target. If no subarray qualifies, return 0.

examples.explanation: The subarray [4, 3] has sum 7 and no single item reaches 7.

constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 1000. 1 <= target <= 10^6. Each item is an integer between 1 and 10^4.
hints: Because every item is positive, adding an item never lowers the sum and removing one never raises it.
Grow the window on the right, and while its sum is at least target, record its length and shrink it from the left.

title: Subarray Product Less Than K
description: Given an array of positive integers and an integer k, return the number of contiguous subarrays whose product of all items is strictly less than k. Subarrays at different positions count separately even when their values are equal.

examples.explanation: The valid subarrays are [10], [5], [2], [6], [10, 5], [5, 2], [2, 6] and [5, 2, 6]. [10, 5, 2] has product 100, which is not less than 100.

constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 1000. Each item is an integer between 1 and 1000. 0 <= k <= 10^6.
hints: If k <= 1 no product can be less than k, because every product is at least 1.
For each right edge, shrink the left edge while the product is at least k, then add right - left + 1 new subarrays that end at the right edge.

title: Maximum Points from Cards
description: A row of cards has a point value on each card. In exactly k moves you take one card per move, each time from either the left end or the right end of the row. Return the maximum total points you can collect.

examples.explanation: Taking the last three cards 5, 6 and 1 gives 12, which beats every other choice.

constraints: 1 <= cardPoints.length <= 1000. 1 <= k <= cardPoints.length. Each value is an integer between 1 and 10^4.
hints: The cards you take always form some cards at the start plus some cards at the end, k in total.
Start with the first k cards, then in each step give up one card from the end of that prefix and take one more card from the end of the row, keeping the best total.

title: Find First and Last Position
description: Given an array of integers sorted in non-decreasing order (duplicates allowed) and a target, return [first, last], the first and last index where the target appears. If the target is not in the array, return [-1, -1]. Aim for O(log n) time.

examples.explanation: The value 8 occupies indexes 3 and 4.

constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 1000. Items and target are integers between -10^6 and 10^6.
hints: Write a helper lowerBound(x) that returns the first index whose value is at least x.
The first position is lowerBound(target) when that index holds the target, and the last position is lowerBound(target + 1) - 1.

title: Search in Sorted Matrix
description: A matrix has rows sorted in ascending order, and the first number of every row is greater than the last number of the row above it. Return true if the target is in the matrix, otherwise false. Aim for O(log(rows * cols)) time.

examples.explanation: 3 is in the first row.

constraints: 0 <= matrix.length <= 100. Every row has the same length, between 1 and 100. Items and target are integers between -10^4 and 10^4.
hints: Read the matrix row by row and it forms one long sorted list.
Binary search over positions 0 to rows * cols - 1, and map position p to row floor(p / cols) and column p % cols.

title: Remove K Digits
description: Given a string num of digits and an integer k, remove exactly k digits so that the remaining number is as small as possible, keeping the relative order of the digits that stay. Return the result as a string without leading zeros, and return "0" if nothing is left or only zeros are left.

examples.explanation: Removing 4, 3 and 2 leaves 1219, the smallest possible number.

constraints: 1 <= num.length <= 1000. num contains digits only and has no leading zeros. 0 <= k <= num.length.
hints: A digit that is larger than the digit after it should be removed first.
Keep a stack of digits, and while k > 0 and the top is larger than the new digit, pop it. When the digits run out, drop the leftover k digits from the end, then strip leading zeros.

title: Longest Mountain in Array
description: A mountain is a contiguous part of the array with at least 3 items that strictly increases up to a peak and then strictly decreases. Return the length of the longest mountain in the array, or 0 if there is none.

examples.explanation: The longest mountain is [1, 4, 7, 3, 2], with peak 7.

constraints: 0 <= arr.length <= 1000. Each item is an integer between 0 and 10^4.
hints: Every mountain has exactly one peak: an item that is larger than both of its neighbours.
For each peak, walk left while the items strictly decrease, and walk right while they strictly decrease, then measure the span.

title: Combination Sum
description: Given an array of distinct positive integers and a target, return every unique combination of the numbers that adds up to the target. A number may be used any number of times. Write each combination in ascending order, and return the combinations sorted lexicographically (compare the first numbers, then the second, and so on). If there is none, return an empty array.

examples.explanation: 2 + 2 + 3 = 7 and 7 = 7 are the only combinations.

constraints: 1 <= candidates.length <= 8. Each candidate is an integer between 2 and 20, and all are distinct. 1 <= target <= 30.
hints: Sort the candidates first so that combinations come out in ascending order.
Recurse with a start index. You may pick the same index again, but never an earlier index, which avoids repeated combinations. Stop a branch when the remaining sum would go below 0.

title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
description: On a phone keypad the digits map to letters: 2 = abc, 3 = def, 4 = ghi, 5 = jkl, 6 = mno, 7 = pqrs, 8 = tuv, 9 = wxyz. Given a string of digits from 2 to 9, return every letter combination it could spell, one letter per digit, sorted in alphabetical order. If the string is empty, return an empty array.

examples.explanation: Each letter of 2 is paired with each letter of 3.

constraints: 0 <= digits.length <= 4. Each character is a digit from 2 to 9.
hints: Store the letters of each digit in an object, and handle the empty string first.
Build the answer one digit at a time: for every existing prefix, append each letter of the next digit. Taking the letters in keypad order keeps the result alphabetical.

title: Palindrome Partitioning
description: Given a string, return every way to split it into consecutive pieces so that every piece is a palindrome. Each way is an array of the pieces in order. List the ways so that a split whose first piece is shorter comes first, and ties are decided by the next piece, and so on.

examples.explanation: Both splits use only palindromic pieces, and the one that starts with the shorter piece a comes first.

constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 12. s contains lowercase letters only.
hints: Recurse on the start position. For each end position, take the piece s[start..end] only if it is a palindrome.
Trying end positions from the shortest piece to the longest gives the required order automatically.

title: Rotate Matrix Clockwise
description: Given a matrix (an array of equal-length rows, not necessarily square), return a new matrix that is the original rotated 90 degrees clockwise. The first row of the input becomes the last column of the result. An empty matrix returns an empty array.

examples.explanation: The first row 1, 2, 3 becomes the last column, read from top to bottom.

constraints: 0 <= rows <= 20. Every row has the same length, between 1 and 20. Items are integers.
hints: A matrix with R rows and C columns turns into one with C rows and R columns.
Result item [r][c] comes from the original item [R - 1 - c][r].

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
description: Given a matrix of integers, return a new matrix in which every row and every column that contains a 0 in the original is filled entirely with 0s. Do not change the input matrix. An empty matrix returns an empty array.

examples.explanation: The 0 sits in row 1 and column 1, so that whole row and that whole column become 0.

constraints: 0 <= rows <= 20. Every row has the same length, between 1 and 20. Items are integers between -1000 and 1000.
hints: First find all rows and columns that contain a 0, using the original matrix only.
Then build the result, writing 0 wherever the row or the column was marked.

title: Interval List Intersections
description: You are given two lists of closed intervals [start, end]. Inside each list the intervals are disjoint and sorted by start. Return the list of intersections between the two lists, sorted. The intersection of two closed intervals is either empty or an interval, and a single shared point such as [5, 5] counts.
constraints: 0 <= a.length, b.length <= 100. Every interval has start <= end, and values are integers between 0 and 10^6.
hints: Use one pointer into each list. The overlap of the two current intervals is [max of starts, min of ends], and it is valid when start <= end.
After checking, move forward the pointer of the interval that ends first, because it cannot overlap anything else.

title: House Robber
description: Houses stand in a row, and house i holds nums[i] units of money. You may rob any set of houses, but you must not rob two houses that are next to each other. Return the largest total you can rob. An empty row gives 0.

examples.explanation: Robbing the houses with 2, 9 and 1 gives 12, and no valid choice gives more.

constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 1000. Each item is an integer between 0 and 1000.
hints: At each house you either rob it (add its money to the best total up to two houses back) or skip it (keep the best total up to the previous house).
Two variables are enough: the best total when the last house is robbed, and the best total when it is skipped.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence Length
description: Given an array of integers, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. A subsequence keeps the original order but does not have to be contiguous. An empty array gives 0.

examples.explanation: One longest subsequence is 2, 3, 7, 101 (or 2, 5, 7, 18).

constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 1000. Each item is an integer between -10^4 and 10^4.
hints: A simple solution keeps, for every index, the length of the best subsequence that ends there, in O(n^2).
For O(n log n) keep an array tails where tails[k] is the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1, and place each number with a binary search.

title: Unique Paths with Obstacles
description: A robot starts at the top-left cell of a grid and wants to reach the bottom-right cell. It can only move right or down. A cell with 1 is an obstacle that cannot be entered, and a cell with 0 is free. Return the number of different paths. If the start or the end is an obstacle, or the grid is empty, return 0.

examples.explanation: The obstacle in the middle leaves two paths: right, right, down, down and down, down, right, right.

constraints: 0 <= rows <= 15. Every row has the same length, between 1 and 15. Each cell is 0 or 1.
hints: The number of ways to reach a free cell is the ways to reach the cell above plus the ways to reach the cell on its left.
An obstacle cell has 0 ways. You can keep one row of counts and update it row by row.

title: Largest Number from Array
description: Given an array of non-negative integers, arrange them in an order that forms the largest possible number when their digits are written one after another. Return that number as a string, because it may be too large for a number. If the result would be all zeros, return "0".

examples.explanation: The order 9, 5, 34, 3, 30 gives the largest value.

constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 100. Each item is an integer between 0 and 10^9.
hints: Compare two numbers a and b as strings: a should come first when a + b is larger than b + a.
Sort with that comparator and join the pieces. If the first character of the result is 0, all numbers were zero.

title: Burst Balloons
description: A row of balloons has a number painted on each one. When you burst balloon i you earn nums[left] * nums[i] * nums[right] coins, where left and right are the nearest balloons that have not burst yet. A missing neighbour counts as a balloon with the number 1. You must burst every balloon, in an order you choose. Return the maximum total coins. An empty row gives 0.
constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 50. Each number is an integer between 0 and 100.
hints: Add a 1 at both ends of the array. Instead of asking which balloon bursts first, ask which balloon in a stretch bursts last.

dp[i][j] is the best score for bursting everything strictly between positions i and j. If k bursts last there, its neighbours are the fixed ends i and j, so dp[i][j] = max over k of dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] + p[i] * p[k] * p[j].

title: Longest Valid Parentheses
description: Given a string made only of the characters ( and ), return the length of the longest contiguous substring that is a valid parentheses string, meaning every ( is closed by a matching ) in the correct order. Return 0 if there is no valid substring.

examples.explanation: The longest valid substring is ()() in the middle.

constraints: 0 <= s.length <= 1000. s contains only ( and ).
hints: Keep a stack of indexes instead of characters, and start it with -1 as a marker for the position just before the current valid stretch.
Push the index of every (. On ), pop; if the stack becomes empty push the current index as the new marker, otherwise the valid length ending here is i minus the index now on top.

title: Distinct Subsequences
description: Given two strings s and t, return the number of distinct subsequences of s that are equal to t. Two subsequences are different when they use different sets of positions in s, even if the letters are the same. If t is longer than s, the answer is 0, and the empty string t has exactly one subsequence.

examples.explanation: Skipping any one of the three b's in rabbbit leaves rabbit, so there are 3 ways.

constraints: 0 <= s.length <= 30 and 0 <= t.length <= 30. Both strings contain lowercase letters only.
hints: Let dp[j] be the number of ways to form the first j letters of t using the letters of s read so far. dp[0] is 1.
For each letter of s, go through j from high to low: if the letter equals t[j - 1], add dp[j - 1] to dp[j]. Going downwards stops a letter of s from being used twice.

title: Maximum Profit in Job Scheduling
description: You are given three arrays of equal length: startTime, endTime and profit. Job i runs from startTime[i] to endTime[i] and pays profit[i]. You may do any set of jobs that do not overlap in time, where a job that ends at time X does not overlap a job that starts at time X. Return the maximum total profit. With no jobs the answer is 0.

examples.explanation: Doing the job from 1 to 3 (profit 50) and then the job from 3 to 6 (profit 70) gives 120.

constraints: 0 <= startTime.length <= 1000. 1 <= startTime[i] < endTime[i] <= 10^6. 1 <= profit[i] <= 10^4.
hints: Sort the jobs by end time. Let best[i] be the best profit using only the first i jobs in that order.
For job i, either skip it (best[i]) or do it, adding its profit to best[c] where c is the number of earlier jobs that end at or before its start. Find c with a binary search over the end times.

title: Longest Increasing Path in Matrix
description: Given a matrix of integers, return the length of the longest strictly increasing path. From a cell you may move up, down, left or right (no diagonals and no wrapping around the edges), and every step must go to a cell with a larger value. An empty matrix returns 0.

examples.explanation: The path 1, 2, 6, 9 goes through four cells.

constraints: 0 <= rows <= 30. Every row has the same length, between 1 and 30. Each value is an integer between -1000 and 1000.
hints: Because every step must increase, a path never visits the same cell twice, so no visited set is needed.
Let longest(r, c) be the longest path that starts at cell (r, c). It is 1 plus the best longest(...) over larger neighbours. Cache each result so that every cell is computed once.

title: Expression Add Operators
description: Given a string num of digits and an integer target, insert the operators +, - or * between some of the digits (or nothing at all, which joins digits into a longer number) so that the expression evaluates to target. Normal precedence applies, so * is done before + and -. A number in the expression must not have a leading zero, so 05 is not allowed but 0 is, and 10 is allowed. Return every valid expression as a string, sorted in default string order.

examples.explanation: 1*2*3 and 1+2+3 both equal 6, and * comes before + in string order.

constraints: 1 <= num.length <= 8. num contains digits only. -10^6 <= target <= 10^6.
hints: Recurse over the position in num. At each step choose the next number (one or more digits, but never a leading zero) and an operator in front of it.
Track the running value and the last term that was added or subtracted. For *, undo that last term and replace it with last * n, which respects precedence without building a parser.

title: Super Egg Drop
description: You have k identical eggs and a building with n floors, numbered 1 to n. There is an unknown critical floor f with 0 <= f <= n: an egg dropped from a floor higher than f breaks, and an egg dropped from floor f or lower survives and can be used again. A broken egg cannot be used again. Return the minimum number of drops that is guaranteed to find f, whatever f turns out to be.

examples.explanation: With one egg you must go floor by floor: drop from floor 1, and if the egg survives, drop from floor 2.

hints: Flip the question: with e eggs and m drops, what is the largest number of floors you can handle?
That number is f(e, m) = f(e - 1, m - 1) + f(e, m - 1) + 1: one drop splits the building into the floors below (egg broke) and the floors above (egg survived). Increase m until f(k, m) >= n.

title: Minimum Number of Refueling Stops
description: A car starts at position 0 and must reach position target, using one unit of fuel per unit of distance. It starts with startFuel units. Gas stations are given as [position, fuel] pairs sorted by position. When the car reaches a station it may stop and add all of that station's fuel to its tank, which has no size limit. A car that arrives with exactly 0 fuel can still refuel at that station. Return the smallest number of stops needed to reach the target, or -1 if it cannot be reached.

examples.explanation: Drive to 10 and take its 60 fuel. Drive to 60 with 10 fuel left and take 40 more, which is enough for the last 40 units. That is 2 stops.

constraints: 1 <= target <= 10^6. 0 <= startFuel <= 10^6. 0 <= stations.length <= 200. Station positions are strictly increasing and less than target. Each station has between 1 and 10^6 fuel.
hints: Let dp[t] be the farthest distance you can reach using exactly t stops. dp[0] is startFuel.

Handle the stations in order. For station i and t from high to low, if dp[t] reaches the station, then dp[t + 1] can be dp[t] plus the station's fuel. The answer is the smallest t with dp[t] >= target.

title: Scramble String
description: A string can be scrambled by this process: if its length is 1, stop. Otherwise split it at some position into two non-empty parts x and y, optionally swap them so the result is x + y or y + x, and then scramble x and y independently using the same process. Return true if s2 can be obtained from s1 this way. The two strings always have the same length.

examples.explanation: great splits into gr and eat. Scrambling gr into rg and keeping eat gives rgeat.

constraints: 1 <= s1.length = s2.length <= 12. Both strings contain lowercase letters only.
hints: Define a function for a pair of equal-length substrings (one of s1, one of s2). Two equal substrings match immediately, and substrings that are not anagrams can never match.

Try every split point k. Either the first k letters of one match the first k of the other and the rests match, or the first k letters of one match the last k of the other (the swapped case) and the rests match. Cache results by start positions and length.

title: Frog Jump
description: A frog crosses a river by jumping from stone to stone. You are given the positions of the stones as a sorted array of distinct non-negative integers, and the frog starts on the first stone, at position 0. The first jump must be exactly 1 unit. If the frog's previous jump was k units, its next jump must be k - 1, k or k + 1 units. The frog only jumps forward, and only onto stones. Return true if the frog can reach the last stone.

examples.explanation: Jumps of 1, 2, 2, 3, 4 and 5 units take the frog 0, 1, 3, 5, 8, 12, 17.

constraints: 1 <= stones.length <= 100. stones[0] = 0 and the positions are strictly increasing, each at most 10^4.
hints: For every stone keep a Set of the jump sizes that can land the frog on it.
Go through the stones from left to right. For each jump size k stored on a stone, try k - 1, k and k + 1 (only positive sizes) and record the size on the stone you land on, if there is one.

title: Rotting Oranges
description: A grid holds 0 (empty cell), 1 (fresh orange) or 2 (rotten orange). Every minute, each fresh orange that is directly up, down, left or right of a rotten orange becomes rotten. Return the number of minutes that must pass until no fresh orange is left, or -1 if some fresh orange can never rot. If there is no fresh orange at the start, the answer is 0.

examples.explanation: The rot spreads outward from the top-left corner one step per minute, and the last orange, in the bottom-right corner, rots in minute 4.

constraints: 1 <= rows, cols <= 10. Each cell is 0, 1 or 2.
hints: Start a breadth-first search from all rotten oranges at the same time, and count the fresh oranges.
Process the search one level at a time, one level per minute. When the queue ends, the answer is the number of minutes if no fresh orange is left, otherwise -1.

title: Is Graph Bipartite
description: An undirected graph with n nodes numbered 0 to n - 1 is given as an adjacency list: graph[i] lists every node connected to node i, and if a is in graph[b] then b is in graph[a]. Return true if the nodes can be split into two groups so that every edge joins one node from each group. The graph may be disconnected and may have no nodes.

examples.explanation: Put nodes 0 and 2 in one group and nodes 1 and 3 in the other. Every edge crosses between the groups.

constraints: 0 <= graph.length <= 100. There are no self-loops and no repeated edges.
hints: Try to color the nodes with two colors so that neighbours always get different colors.
Run a breadth-first search from every node that is not colored yet (the graph may be disconnected). If you meet a neighbour with the same color as the current node, the answer is false.

title: Redundant Connection
description: A tree with nodes numbered 1 to n had one extra edge added, so the input is a list of n edges [a, b], each joining two different nodes, and the graph is connected. Return an edge that can be removed so that the remaining edges form a tree. If several edges qualify, return the one that appears last in the input.

examples.explanation: The three edges form a cycle, and removing the last one leaves a tree.

constraints: 3 <= edges.length <= 100. Every edge joins two different nodes between 1 and edges.length, and there are no repeated edges.
hints: Add the edges one at a time, keeping track of which nodes are already connected.
With union-find, the first edge whose two ends already have the same root is the edge that closes the cycle, and it is the last cycle edge in the input order.

title: Binary Tree Right Side View
description: A binary tree is given in level order as an array: the nodes are listed row by row from left to right, null marks a missing child, and a missing node has no children listed under it. An empty array is an empty tree. Return the values you would see standing on the right side of the tree, from top to bottom, which is the last node of each level.

examples.explanation: The last node of the levels is 1, then 3, then 4.

constraints: 0 <= tree.length <= 100. Node values are integers between -1000 and 1000.
hints: First build node objects from the array: use a queue, and give every dequeued node its next two array items as left and right children.
Then walk the tree level by level and keep the last node of each level.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of Binary Tree
description: A binary tree with distinct values is given in level order as an array: the nodes are listed row by row from left to right, null marks a missing child, and a missing node has no children listed under it. Given two values p and q that both exist in the tree, return the value of their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both p and q in its subtree, where a node counts as being in its own subtree.

examples.explanation: 5 is in the left subtree of 3 and 1 is in the right subtree, so the lowest common ancestor is the root 3.

constraints: 2 <= tree.length <= 100. Node values are distinct integers between -1000 and 1000. p and q are different values that both appear in the tree.
hints: Build node objects from the array first, then search the tree recursively.
A call returns the node if it is p or q, otherwise whatever the two sides return. If both sides return something, the current node is the answer.

title: K Closest Points to Origin
description: Given an array of points [x, y] and an integer k, return the k points closest to the origin (0, 0) by straight-line distance. Order the returned points from closest to farthest. Points at the same distance are ordered by x, and then by y, both from smaller to larger.

examples.explanation: The squared distances are 18, 26 and 20, so the two closest are [3, 3] and [-2, 4].

constraints: 0 <= k <= points.length <= 1000. Coordinates are integers between -10^4 and 10^4.
hints: You can compare squared distances x * x + y * y, which avoids square roots and rounding.
Sorting all points costs O(n log n) and passes. A max-heap holding only the k best points so far brings it down to O(n log k).

title: Minimum Cost to Connect Sticks
description: You have sticks with the given lengths. Joining any two sticks into one costs the sum of their lengths, and the new stick has that length. Keep joining until a single stick is left. Return the minimum total cost. If there are 0 or 1 sticks, the cost is 0.

examples.explanation: Join 2 and 3 for 5, then join 5 and 4 for 9. The total is 5 + 9 = 14.

constraints: 0 <= sticks.length <= 1000. Each length is an integer between 1 and 10^4.
hints: Always joining the two shortest sticks keeps the repeated additions as small as possible.
Use a min-heap: take the two smallest values, add their sum to the cost, and push the sum back. Stop when one stick is left.

title: Replace Words with Roots
description: You are given a list of root words and a sentence whose words are separated by single spaces. Replace every word of the sentence that starts with a root by the shortest root that is a prefix of it. A word that starts with none of the roots stays unchanged. Return the new sentence.

examples.input: roots = ["cat", "bat", "rat"], sentence = "the cattle was rattled by the battery"
examples.output: "the cat was rat by the bat"
examples.explanation: cattle, rattled and battery are replaced by their roots cat, rat and bat. The other words have no root.

constraints: 0 <= roots.length <= 100. 1 <= sentence.length <= 1000. Roots and words contain lowercase letters only, and words are separated by single spaces.
hints: Store the roots in a Set, or in a trie to be faster on long words.
For each word try its prefixes from the shortest to the longest, and use the first one that is a root.

input: the cattle was rattled by the battery
tests.output: the cat was rat by the bat

title: Trie Prefix Counts Simulation
description: Simulate a word store. Each operation is ["insert", word] (add one copy of the word), ["erase", word] (remove one copy if the word is present, otherwise do nothing) or ["count", prefix] (how many stored copies start with the prefix). The same word can be stored several times, and every copy counts. Return the results of the "count" operations, in order.

examples.explanation: Both stored words start with app, so the first count is 2. After apple is erased the count is 1. Nothing starts with b.

constraints: 0 <= operations.length <= 1000. Words and prefixes are non-empty strings of lowercase letters, at most 20 characters.
hints: Make each trie node store how many stored words pass through it. The count of a prefix is the count of the node you reach by following it.
Keep a Map from word to number of copies, so that erasing a word that is not stored does nothing.

title: Coin Change Minimum Coins
description: Given an array of coin denominations and a target amount, return the minimum number of coins needed to make exactly that amount. Each coin can be used any number of times. Return -1 if the amount cannot be formed.
constraints: Coin values are positive integers. amount is a non-negative integer.
expected_complexity: O(amount * number of coins) time and O(amount) space
hints: Let dp[x] represent the minimum number of coins needed to make amount x.
Build the table from smaller amounts toward the target.
For each coin, consider using it as the final coin.

title: Decode Ways
description: A message containing digits can be decoded using 1 through 26 as mappings to letters A through Z. Return the number of possible decodings of the given digit string.
constraints: The string contains only digits and has length between 1 and 100.
hints: A single non-zero digit can represent one letter.
A valid two-digit number must be between 10 and 26.
Use the number of ways to decode the previous one and two positions.

title: Word Break
description: Given a string and a dictionary of words, determine whether the string can be segmented into one or more dictionary words.
constraints: The string length is at most 300. Dictionary words contain lowercase English letters.
expected_complexity: O(n * m * k) time in the worst case and O(n) space
hints: Use dp[i] to indicate whether the prefix ending at index i can be segmented.
Store dictionary words in a Set for fast lookup.
For each position, try possible previous word boundaries.

title: Target Sum Ways
description: Given a list of non-negative integers, assign either a plus or minus sign to every number so that the resulting expression equals target. Return the number of different assignments that achieve the target.
constraints: Numbers are non-negative integers. The array length is at most 20.
expected_complexity: O(n * sum(nums)) time and O(sum(nums)) space
hints: Separate the numbers assigned a plus sign from those assigned a minus sign.
This can be transformed into a subset-sum counting problem.
If (sum + target) is odd or outside the possible range, no solution exists.

title: Longest Common Subsequence
description: Given two strings, return the length of their longest subsequence that appears in both strings while preserving relative character order.
constraints: Both strings contain lowercase English letters and have length at most 1000.
expected_complexity: O(m * n) time and O(min(m, n)) space
hints: Compare the final characters of the two prefixes.
If they match, extend the best solution for the previous prefixes.
Otherwise take the better result from skipping one character from either string.

title: Edit Distance
description: Given two strings, return the minimum number of insertions, deletions, and substitutions required to transform the first string into the second.
constraints: Strings contain lowercase English letters and have length at most 500.
expected_complexity: O(m * n) time and O(min(m, n)) space
hints: Use a DP row representing distances to prefixes of the second string.
Equal characters require no new operation.
For different characters, consider insert, delete, and replace.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
description: Given an integer array, find the contiguous subarray with the largest product and return that product.
constraints: The array contains at least one integer.
hints: Track both the largest and smallest product ending at the current position.
A negative number can turn the smallest product into the largest.
Update the global maximum after processing each element.

title: Daily Temperatures
description: Given daily temperatures, return an array where each position contains the number of days that must pass until a warmer temperature occurs. Return 0 when no warmer future day exists.
constraints: The array length is at most 100000.
hints: Keep indices whose warmer day has not been found.
Maintain a decreasing stack of temperatures.
When the current temperature is warmer, resolve previous indices.

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
description: Given an array of non-negative bar heights representing a histogram, return the area of the largest rectangle that can be formed using consecutive bars.
constraints: The array length is at most 100000.
hints: Maintain indices of bars in increasing height order.
When a shorter bar appears, previously stored bars can no longer extend farther right.
Use the current index as the right boundary and the new stack top as the left boundary.

title: Sliding Window Maximum
description: Given an integer array and a window size k, return the maximum value in every contiguous window of size k.
constraints: The array length is at most 100000. 1 <= k <= nums.length.
expected_complexity: O(n) time and O(k) auxiliary space
hints: Store indices rather than values so expired elements can be removed.
Maintain a decreasing deque of candidate indices.
The index at the front of the deque is the maximum for the current window.

title: Trapping Rain Water
description: Given an array of non-negative bar heights, calculate how much rain water can be trapped between the bars.
constraints: The array length is at most 100000.
hints: Water above a position depends on the shorter of the tallest boundaries on both sides.
Use two pointers starting at both ends.
Process the side with the smaller current boundary.

title: Minimum Window Substring
description: Given strings s and t, return the shortest substring of s that contains every character in t with at least the required frequency. Return an empty string if no such substring exists.
constraints: The strings contain English letters. The length of s is at most 100000.
hints: Count the required frequency of every character in t.
Expand the right edge until the window contains all required characters.
Then shrink the left edge while keeping the window valid.

title: Word Ladder Length
description: Given a begin word, an end word, and a dictionary, return the number of words in the shortest transformation sequence from beginWord to endWord. Each transformation changes exactly one character and every intermediate word must exist in the dictionary.
constraints: All words have the same length and contain lowercase English letters.
expected_complexity: O(n * L^2) time and O(n) space
hints: Use breadth-first search because every transformation has equal cost.
Generate all words that differ by one character.
Mark words visited when they enter the queue.

title: Course Schedule Feasibility
description: There are numCourses courses numbered from 0 to numCourses - 1. prerequisites contains pairs [course, prerequisite]. Return true if all courses can be completed, or false if the prerequisites contain a cycle.
constraints: numCourses is positive. Each prerequisite pair contains valid course indices.
expected_complexity: O(V + E) time and O(V + E) space
hints: Model prerequisites as directed edges.
A cycle prevents a complete topological ordering.
Use indegrees and a queue to process courses with no remaining prerequisites.

title: Number of Islands
description: Given a grid containing '1' for land and '0' for water, return the number of connected islands. Cells are connected horizontally or vertically.
constraints: The grid has at most 200 rows and 200 columns.
expected_complexity: O(rows * columns) time and O(rows * columns) space in the worst case
hints: When an unvisited land cell is found, start a traversal from it.
Mark every connected land cell as visited.
Each traversal corresponds to one island.

title: Kth Largest Element
description: Given an integer array and an integer k, return the kth largest element in the array.
constraints: The array contains at least one integer. 1 <= k <= nums.length.
expected_complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space
hints: Sorting the array in descending order makes the kth largest element easy to locate.
Duplicates count as separate positions.
Be careful to return the kth largest rather than the kth distinct value.

title: Find Duplicate Number
description: Given an array containing n + 1 integers where each integer is between 1 and n inclusive, return the single duplicated number. The duplicate may appear more than twice.
constraints: The array contains n + 1 integers with values from 1 through n. There is exactly one duplicated value.
expected_complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space
hints: Treat each value as a pointer to another index.
The duplicate creates a cycle.
Use Floyd's tortoise and hare cycle detection.

title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
description: Given a binary tree represented as a level-order array where null represents a missing child, serialize the tree and then deserialize it. Return the resulting tree in the same normalized level-order array representation.
constraints: The input represents a valid binary tree in level-order form. Values are integers or null. The tree contains at most 100000 nodes.
hints: Use a queue to reconstruct the tree from the level-order representation.
Preserve null children while traversing the tree.
Remove only trailing null values from the final level-order representation.
